verses.text: In the first year of King Cyrus of Persia, the LORD fulfilled his word through Jeremiah by stirring Cyrus to send out a proclamation throughout his kingdom and put it in writing.
"This is what King Cyrus of Persia says: 'The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He has charged me with building a house for him in Jerusalem, in Judah.
If any of his people are among you, may their God be with them. Let them go up to Jerusalem in Judah and rebuild the house of the LORD, the God of Israel, the God who is in Jerusalem.
Let the neighbors of anyone who remains, wherever they live, help them with silver, gold, goods, and livestock, in addition to voluntary gifts for God's house in Jerusalem.'"
Then the family heads of Judah and Benjamin and the priests and Levites got ready to go. God had stirred them to go up and rebuild the LORD's house in Jerusalem.
Their neighbors supported them with silver vessels, gold, goods, livestock, and valuables, along with everything they gave as voluntary offerings.
King Cyrus also brought out the vessels of the LORD's house that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and put in the temple of his own gods.
King Cyrus of Persia had Mithredath the treasurer bring them out and count them out to Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah.
Here is what was counted: thirty gold platters, a thousand silver platters, and twenty-nine knives,
thirty gold bowls, four hundred ten silver bowls of another kind, and a thousand other vessels.
In all there were fifty-four hundred gold and silver vessels. Sheshbazzar brought them all up from Babylon to Jerusalem when the exiles returned.
Here are the people of the province who returned from exile. King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had taken them to Babylon, and they came back to Jerusalem and Judah, each to their own town.
They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah. Here is the count of the Israelite men.
Parosh's descendants numbered two thousand one hundred seventy-two.
Shephatiah's descendants numbered three hundred seventy-two.
Arah's descendants numbered seven hundred seventy-five.
Pahathmoab's descendants from the families of Jeshua and Joab numbered two thousand eight hundred twelve.
Elam's descendants numbered one thousand two hundred fifty-four.
Zattu's descendants numbered nine hundred forty-five.
Zaccai's descendants numbered seven hundred sixty.
Bani's descendants numbered six hundred forty-two.
Bebai's descendants numbered six hundred twenty-three.
Azgad's descendants numbered one thousand two hundred twenty-two.
Adonikam's descendants numbered six hundred sixty-six.
Bigvai's descendants numbered two thousand fifty-six.
Adin's descendants numbered four hundred fifty-four.
Ater's descendants through Hezekiah numbered ninety-eight.
Bezai's descendants numbered three hundred twenty-three.
Jorah's descendants numbered one hundred twelve.
Hashum's descendants numbered two hundred twenty-three.
Gibbar's descendants numbered ninety-five.
From Bethlehem came one hundred twenty-three.
From Netophah came fifty-six.
From Anathoth came one hundred twenty-eight.
From Azmaveth came forty-two.
From Kiriath Arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth came seven hundred forty-three.
From Ramah and Geba came six hundred twenty-one.
From Michmas came one hundred twenty-two.
From Bethel and Ai came two hundred twenty-three.
From Nebo came fifty-two.
Magbish's descendants numbered one hundred fifty-six.
the other Elam's descendants numbered one thousand two hundred fifty-four.
Harim's descendants numbered three hundred twenty.
From Lod, Hadid, and Ono came seven hundred twenty-five.
From Jericho came three hundred forty-five.
From Senaah came three thousand six hundred thirty.
The priests included nine hundred seventy-three descendants of Jedaiah from the family of Jeshua.
Immer's descendants numbered one thousand fifty-two.
Pashhur's descendants numbered one thousand two hundred forty-seven.
Harim's descendants numbered one thousand seventeen.
The Levites included seventy-four descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel from the family of Hodaviah.
The singers were Asaph's descendants, a hundred twenty-eight in all.
The gatekeepers came from the families of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai. They numbered a hundred thirty-nine in all.
The temple servants came from the families of Ziha, Hasupha, and Tabbaoth,
Keros, Siaha, Padon,
Lebanah, Hagabah, Akkub,
Hagab, Shamlai, Hanan,
Giddel, Gahar, Reaiah,
Rezin, Nekoda, Gazzam,
Uzza, Paseah, Besai,
Asnah, Meunim, Nephisim,
Bakbuk, Hakupha, Harhur,
Bazluth, Mehida, Harsha,
Barkos, Sisera, Temah,
Neziah and Hatipha.
The descendants of Solomon's servants came from the families of Sotai, Hassophereth, and Peruda,
Jaalah, Darkon, Giddel,
Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth Hazzebaim, and Ami.
The temple servants and the descendants of Solomon's servants numbered three hundred ninety-two altogether.
Some people returned from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer without records to establish their ancestry or show whether they belonged to Israel.
They included the descendants of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda, six hundred fifty-two in all.
The priestly families included the descendants of Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai. Barzillai had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite and taken the family's name.
They looked for their names in the family records, but their names were missing. So they were disqualified from serving as priests.
The governor told them to refrain from eating the most sacred food until a priest could make a ruling using the Urim and Thummim.
The whole assembly numbered forty-two thousand three hundred sixty,
plus seven thousand three hundred thirty-seven male and female servants. They also had two hundred men and women who sang.
They had seven hundred thirty-six horses and two hundred forty-five mules,
as well as four hundred thirty-five camels and six thousand seven hundred twenty donkeys.
When they arrived at the LORD's house in Jerusalem, some family heads gave freely to rebuild God's house on its original site.
They gave what they could to the building fund: sixty-one thousand darics of gold, five thousand minas of silver, and a hundred priestly garments.
The priests, Levites, some of the people, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants settled in their own towns. The rest of Israel settled in their towns too.
By the seventh month, the Israelites had settled in their towns, and the people came together in Jerusalem as one.

Jeshua son of Jozadak and his fellow priests, along with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his relatives, set to work and built the altar of the God of Israel. They did this to present burnt offerings on it, as written in the law of Moses, the man of God.
Although they were afraid of the people of the surrounding lands, they set the altar on its original base and presented burnt offerings to the LORD on it every morning and evening.
They celebrated the Festival of Booths as written, presenting each day's prescribed number of burnt offerings.
After that they brought the regular burnt offerings, the offerings for the new moons and all the LORD's sacred festivals, and the gifts of everyone who wanted to give freely to the LORD.
They began presenting burnt offerings to the LORD on the first day of the seventh month, even before the foundation of the LORD's temple had been laid.

They paid the stoneworkers and carpenters and gave food, drink, and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre to ship cedar from Lebanon by sea to Joppa, under the authorization King Cyrus of Persia had given them.

In the second month of the second year after they came to God's house in Jerusalem, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Jeshua son of Jozadak, their fellow priests and Levites, and everyone who had returned to Jerusalem from exile began the work. They put Levites twenty years old and up in charge of work on the LORD's house.

Jeshua and his sons and brothers, Kadmiel and his sons from the family of Judah, and the Levites of Henadad's family with their sons and brothers worked together to supervise the builders at God's house.

When the builders laid the foundation of the LORD's temple, the priests took their places in their robes with trumpets. The Levites from Asaph's family stood with cymbals to praise the LORD, following the instructions of King David of Israel.

They sang back and forth in praise and thanks to the LORD: "He is good, and his faithful love for Israel lasts forever." All the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD because the foundation of his house had been laid.
Many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept aloud as they watched the foundation of this house being laid. Many others shouted with joy.
The people couldn't tell the sound of joyful shouting from the sound of weeping. They made so much noise that it could be heard far away.
The enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel.
They approached Zerubbabel and the family heads and said, "Let us build with you. We seek your God just as you do. We've been sacrificing to him since King Esar Haddon of Assyria brought us here."

Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the other heads of Israel's families answered, "You have no share in building a house for our God. We'll build it ourselves for the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus of Persia commanded us."
Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made it difficult for them to build.
They hired advisers to work against them and block their plans throughout the reign of King Cyrus of Persia and into the reign of King Darius of Persia.
At the beginning of Ahasuerus's reign, they wrote an accusation against the people of Judah and Jerusalem.
In Artaxerxes' time, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and their associates wrote to King Artaxerxes of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic script and delivered in the Aramaic language.
Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the secretary wrote a letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes, as follows.
It came from Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the secretary, and their associates: the Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, Apharsites, Archevites, Babylonians, Shushanchites, Dehaites, and Elamites,
and the other peoples whom the great and noble Osnappar had moved and settled in Samaria and elsewhere in the province Beyond the River.
This is a copy of the letter they sent: "To King Artaxerxes, from your servants in the province Beyond the River.
Let the king know that the Jews who left your territory have come to Jerusalem. They're rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They've finished its walls and repaired its foundations.
Let the king also know that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, the people will stop paying tribute, customs, and tolls. In the end the kings will lose revenue.
Since we owe our living to the palace, we can't stand by and watch the king be dishonored. So we're writing to inform you

and ask that you search your ancestors' records. You'll find that this city has a history of rebellion and has brought trouble to kings and provinces. People have stirred up revolts there before. That's why the city was destroyed.
We warn the king that if this city is rebuilt and the walls are finished, you'll lose control of the province Beyond the River."
Then the king replied: "To Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the secretary, and their associates living in Samaria and elsewhere in the province Beyond the River. Peace.
The letter you sent us has been read aloud clearly to me.
I ordered a search, and it confirmed that this city has risen against kings before and has been the site of rebellion and revolt.
Powerful kings have ruled from Jerusalem over the whole province Beyond the River, and they received tribute, customs, and tolls.
Issue an order now to stop these men. The city must stay as it is until I issue another decree.
See that you do this promptly. Why let the damage grow and harm the kings?"
As soon as a copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read to Rehum, Shimshai the secretary, and their associates, they hurried to the Jews in Jerusalem and forced them to stop.
Then work on God's house in Jerusalem came to a halt. It remained stopped until the second year of King Darius of Persia.
The prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo spoke to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel.
Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak set to work rebuilding God's house in Jerusalem. God's prophets were there helping them.

At the same time Tattenai, the governor of the province Beyond the River, came with Shetharbozenai and their associates. They asked the builders, "Who gave you permission to rebuild this house and finish this wall?"
They also asked for the names of the men working on the building.
But God was watching over the Jewish elders. The officials let them keep working while they reported the matter to Darius and waited for his written answer.
Here is a copy of the letter to King Darius from Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, Shetharbozenai, and their Apharsachite associates in that province.
They wrote, "To King Darius, may you have peace in every way.

We want the king to know that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. The people are building it with large stones and setting timber in the walls. They are working diligently, and the work is going well.
We asked the elders, 'Who gave you permission to rebuild this house and finish this wall?'
We also asked for their names so we could give you a written list of the men in charge.
They answered us, 'We serve the God of heaven and earth. We're rebuilding the house that stood here many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and completed.
Our ancestors provoked the God of heaven to anger. He handed them over to Nebuchadnezzar the Chaldean, king of Babylon, who destroyed this house and took the people away to Babylon.
But in the first year of Cyrus as king of Babylon, he issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.

Nebuchadnezzar had taken the gold and silver vessels from God's house in Jerusalem and put them in the temple in Babylon. King Cyrus took those vessels out of the Babylonian temple and gave them to Sheshbazzar, whom he had appointed governor.
Cyrus told him, "Take these vessels and put them back in the temple in Jerusalem. Rebuild God's house on its original site."
So Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of God's house in Jerusalem. Building has gone on since then, and the house still isn't finished.'

Now if it pleases the king, have a search made of the royal treasury in Babylon to see whether King Cyrus issued a decree to rebuild this house of God in Jerusalem. Then please tell us what you want done about this."
King Darius gave the order, and the archives where Babylon kept its treasures were searched.
A scroll was found at Achmetha in the palace in the province of Media. It contained this record:

"In his first year as king, Cyrus issued this decree about God's house in Jerusalem: Rebuild the house as a place where sacrifices are offered. Lay a strong foundation. The building is to be sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide,
with three rows of large stones and one row of new timber. The royal treasury is to pay the costs.
Return the gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem to Babylon. Put them back in their places in God's house in Jerusalem."
So now, Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, Shetharbozenai, and your Apharsachite associates in that province, keep away from the site.
Leave the work on God's house alone. Let the Jewish governor and elders rebuild it on its original site.

I also decree what you must do for these Jewish elders as they rebuild God's house: pay their expenses promptly and in full from the royal revenue collected in the province Beyond the River, so the work can go ahead without delay.
Give them whatever the priests in Jerusalem ask for: bulls, rams, and lambs for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, as well as wheat, salt, wine, and oil. Provide it every day without fail,
so they can offer sacrifices with a pleasing aroma to the God of heaven and pray for the lives of the king and his sons.

I also decree that if anyone changes this order, a beam is to be pulled from that person's house and the person lifted up and fastened to it. Their house is to be made a pile of refuse for this offense.
May the God who has put his name there overthrow any king or people who would change this decree and destroy God's house in Jerusalem. I, Darius, issue this decree. Carry it out promptly.
Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, Shetharbozenai, and their associates promptly did what King Darius had ordered.

The Jewish elders made good progress with the building, encouraged by the words of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo. They finished building it according to the command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes king of Persia.
The house was completed on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of King Darius's reign.
The Israelites, the priests, the Levites, and the rest of the returned exiles celebrated the dedication of God's house with joy.
For the dedication they offered a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, and four hundred lambs, as well as twelve male goats as a sin offering for all Israel, one for each tribe.
They organized the priests by division and the Levites by their assigned groups to serve God in Jerusalem, as written in the Book of Moses.
The returned exiles celebrated Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month.
The priests and Levites had purified themselves together, so they were all clean. The Levites slaughtered the Passover animals for the returned exiles, for their fellow priests, and for themselves.

The Israelites who had returned from exile ate the meal, along with everyone who had joined them and turned away from the unclean practices of the surrounding nations to seek the LORD, the God of Israel.

They celebrated the Festival of Unleavened Bread for seven days with joy. The LORD had made them glad by turning the heart of the king of Assyria toward them so that he supported their work on the house of God, the God of Israel.
After these events, during the reign of King Artaxerxes of Persia, there was a man named Ezra. His father was Seraiah, whose line went back through Azariah and Hilkiah,
then through Shallum, Zadok, and Ahitub,
through Amariah, Azariah, and Meraioth,
through Zerahiah, Uzzi, and Bukki,
and through Abishua, Phinehas, and Eleazar to Aaron the chief priest.

Ezra came up from Babylon. He was a scribe who knew the law of Moses well, the law the LORD, the God of Israel, had given. The king granted everything Ezra asked for because the hand of the LORD his God was on him.
In the seventh year of King Artaxerxes, some Israelites went up to Jerusalem, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants.
Ezra arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the king's seventh year.
He set out from Babylon on the first day of the first month and reached Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month because God's good hand was on him.
Ezra had devoted himself to studying and obeying the LORD's law and teaching its statutes and rulings in Israel.
This is a copy of the letter King Artaxerxes gave Ezra the priest and scribe, who was trained in the LORD's commands and statutes for Israel.
"From Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, scribe of the law of the perfect God of heaven.
I decree that any Israelites in my kingdom, including priests and Levites, who freely choose to go to Jerusalem may go with you.
The king and his seven advisers are sending you to inquire about Judah and Jerusalem according to the law of your God that you have with you.
Take the silver and gold that the king and his advisers have freely given to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem.
Take also any silver and gold you receive throughout the province of Babylon, along with what the people and priests willingly give for the house of their God in Jerusalem.
Use this money promptly to buy bulls, rams, and lambs, with the proper grain and drink offerings. Offer them on the altar at the house of your God in Jerusalem.
You and your fellow Israelites may use the remaining silver and gold as you see fit, in keeping with the will of your God.
Deliver the vessels entrusted to you for service in your God's house before the God of Jerusalem.
If you need to provide anything else for your God's house, pay for it from the royal treasury.
I, King Artaxerxes, order all the treasurers of the province Beyond the River to promptly supply whatever Ezra the priest and scribe of the law of the God of heaven asks for,
up to a hundred talents of silver, a hundred cors of wheat, a hundred baths of wine, and a hundred baths of oil, with no limit on salt.
Do whatever the God of heaven commands for his house, exactly as ordered. Why should anger fall on the kingdom of the king and his sons?
You should also know that you have no authority to collect tribute, customs, or tolls from any priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, or other workers at this house of God.
Ezra, use the wisdom your God has given you to appoint magistrates and judges over the people of the province Beyond the River who know your God's laws. Teach those who don't know them.
Anyone who refuses to obey the law of your God and the king's law must be judged promptly, whether the sentence is death, exile, seizure of property, or imprisonment."
Praise the LORD, the God of our ancestors, who put it in the king's heart to honor and beautify the LORD's house in Jerusalem.

He showed me faithful love in the presence of the king, his advisers, and his most powerful officials. The hand of the LORD my God gave me courage, and I gathered leaders from Israel to go up with me.
Here are the heads of the families and the family records of those who came up with me from Babylon during the reign of King Artaxerxes.
From Phinehas's descendants came Gershom, from Ithamar's descendants Daniel, and from David's descendants Hattush.
From the descendants of Shecaniah in Parosh's family came Zechariah, with a hundred fifty men listed with him in the family records.
From Pahathmoab's family came Eliehoenai son of Zerahiah, with two hundred men.
From Shecaniah's family came the son of Jahaziel, with three hundred men.
From Adin's family came Ebed son of Jonathan, with fifty men.
From Elam's family came Jeshaiah son of Athaliah, with seventy men.
From Shephatiah's family came Zebadiah son of Michael, with eighty men.
From Joab's family came Obadiah son of Jehiel, with two hundred eighteen men.
From Shelomith's family came the son of Josiphiah, with a hundred sixty men.
From Bebai's family came Zechariah son of Bebai, with twenty-eight men.
From Azgad's family came Johanan son of Hakkatan, with a hundred ten men.
The last to come from Adonikam's family were Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah, with sixty men.
From Bigvai's family came Uthai and Zabbud, with seventy men.
I gathered them by the river that flows to Ahava, and we camped there for three days. When I looked through the people and the priests, I found no Levites.
So I sent for the leaders Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, and for the teachers Joiarib and Elnathan.
I sent them to Iddo, the leader at Casiphia, and told them what to say to Iddo and his fellow temple servants there. I asked them to send us people to serve in the house of our God.
Because the good hand of our God was on us, they brought us Sherebiah, a man of good judgment descended from Mahli, son of Levi, son of Israel. His sons and brothers came with him, eighteen in all.
They also brought Hashabiah and Jeshaiah from Merari's family, together with their brothers and sons, twenty in all.
They sent two hundred twenty temple servants from the group David and the officials had assigned to assist the Levites. Every one of them was listed by name.
There by the Ahava River I called for a fast so we could humble ourselves before our God and ask him for a safe journey for us, our children, and everything we owned.

I was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen to protect us from enemies on the road. We'd told the king, "Our God's hand is on all who seek him, for their good. His power and anger are against everyone who abandons him."
So we fasted and pleaded with our God for safe passage, and he answered us.
Then I set apart twelve leading priests, including Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers.
I weighed out to them the silver, gold, and vessels that the king, his advisers, his officials, and the Israelites there had given for our God's house.
I handed over six hundred fifty talents of silver, a hundred talents of silver vessels, and a hundred talents of gold.
I also gave them twenty gold bowls weighing a thousand darics and two vessels of fine polished bronze, as valuable as gold.
I told them, "You are set apart for the LORD, and these vessels are set apart too. The silver and gold are a voluntary offering to the LORD, the God of your ancestors.
Guard them until you weigh them out in the rooms of the LORD's house in Jerusalem before the leading priests, Levites, and heads of Israel's families."
The priests and Levites took charge of the silver, gold, and vessels that had been weighed, to bring them to the house of our God in Jerusalem.
We left the Ahava River for Jerusalem on the twelfth day of the first month. Our God's hand was on us, and he protected us from enemies and bandits on the road.
We arrived in Jerusalem and rested there for three days.

On the fourth day the silver, gold, and vessels were weighed in God's house and entrusted to Meremoth son of Uriah the priest. Eleazar son of Phinehas was with him, along with the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui.
Everything was counted and weighed, and the weights were recorded at the time.

The returned exiles brought offerings to the God of Israel: twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering. All these were presented to the LORD as a burnt offering.
They delivered the king's orders to the royal governors and to the governors of the province Beyond the River, who then supported the people and God's house.

After these things were done, the leaders came to me and said, "The people of Israel, including the priests and Levites, have failed to keep themselves separate from the peoples of the land and have followed their detestable practices. These are the practices of the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites.

They've married women from these peoples and taken wives from among them for their sons. In this way the people set apart as holy have intermarried with the peoples of the land. The leaders and officials were the first to act unfaithfully."
When I heard this, I tore my clothes and my robe, pulled hair from my head and beard, and sat down in shock.
All who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around me because of the unfaithfulness of the returned exiles. I sat there stunned until the evening offering.
At the evening offering I got up from where I had been sitting in humiliation, my clothes and robe still torn. I fell to my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God.
I prayed, "My God, I'm too ashamed to lift my face to you. Our sins have risen over our heads, and our guilt reaches the heavens.

From our ancestors' time to this very day, our guilt has been great. Because of our sins, we and our kings and priests were handed over to foreign kings, to the sword, captivity, plunder, and public shame, as we still see today.
For a brief moment the LORD our God has shown us grace. He's let some of us escape and given us a secure place in his sanctuary, bringing light to our eyes and a little relief in our bondage.

We're still servants, yet our God hasn't abandoned us in our bondage. He's shown us steadfast love before the kings of Persia, giving us new life so we could rebuild our God's house, restore its ruins, and have protection in Judah and Jerusalem.
Now, our God, what can we say after all this? We've abandoned the commands

you gave through your servants the prophets: 'The land you're going to take possession of has been defiled by the peoples who live there. Their detestable practices have filled it with uncleanness from one end to the other.

So don't give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters for your sons. Don't seek their peace or prosperity. Then you'll be strong, enjoy the good things the land produces, and pass it on to your children forever.'
After all that has happened to us because of our evil deeds and great guilt, you, our God, have punished us less than our sins deserve and let this remnant survive.
Should we break your commands again and intermarry with the peoples who do these detestable things? Wouldn't you be angry enough to destroy us, leaving no remnant and no survivors?
LORD, God of Israel, you are righteous. You've left us alive as a remnant, as we are today. Here we are before you in our guilt. Because of it, none of us can stand before you."
While Ezra prayed and confessed, weeping and lying face down in front of God's house, a large crowd of Israelite men, women, and children gathered around him. They too wept bitterly.
Shecaniah son of Jehiel, from Elam's family, said to Ezra, "We've been unfaithful to our God by marrying foreign women from the peoples of the land. Even now there is hope for Israel.

Let's make a covenant with our God to send away all these wives and the children born to them, following your advice and the advice of those who tremble at our God's command. Let it be done according to the law.
Get up. This is your responsibility, and we are with you. Take courage and do it."
Ezra got up and made the leading priests, the Levites, and all Israel swear to do what had been proposed. They took the oath.
Ezra left the front of God's house and went to the room of Jehohanan son of Eliashib. He ate no food and drank no water there because he was mourning the unfaithfulness of the returned exiles.
They sent out a proclamation across Judah and Jerusalem calling all the returned exiles to gather in Jerusalem.
By decision of the officials and elders, anyone who failed to come within three days would lose all their property and be excluded from the assembly of the returned exiles.

Within three days the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered in Jerusalem. It was the twentieth day of the ninth month. All the people sat in the square in front of God's house, trembling because of the matter at hand and the heavy rain.
Ezra the priest stood up and said, "You've been unfaithful by marrying foreign women, adding to Israel's guilt.
Now confess to the LORD, the God of your ancestors, and do what pleases him. Separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from the foreign women you married."
The whole assembly replied loudly, "We must do as you say.
But there are many people here, and it's the rainy season. We can't stand outside. This can't be settled in a day or two, because so many of us have been unfaithful in this matter.

Let our officials act on behalf of the whole assembly. Let each man in our towns who has married a foreign woman come at an appointed time with his town's elders and judges, until the matter is settled and our God's fierce anger turns away from us."
Only Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah opposed the plan, with Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite supporting them.
The returned exiles went ahead with the plan. Ezra the priest and certain family heads chosen by name from their respective families sat down on the first day of the tenth month to examine the cases.
By the first day of the first month they had finished reviewing the cases of all the men who had married foreign women.
Among the priests' descendants who had married foreign women were Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah from the family of Jeshua son of Jozadak and his brothers.
They pledged to send their wives away and offered a ram from the flock as a guilt offering.
From Immer's family came Hanani and Zebadiah.
From Harim's family came Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah.
From Pashhur's family came Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah.
The Levites listed were Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (also called Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer.
Among the singers was Eliashib. Among the gatekeepers were Shallum, Telem, and Uri.
Among the other Israelites, Parosh's family included Ramiah, Izziah, Malchijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Malchijah, and Benaiah.
Elam's family included Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah.
Zattu's family included Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza.
Bebai's family included Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai.
Bani's family included Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth.
Pahathmoab's family included Adna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh.
Harim's family included Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, Shimeon,
and Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah.
Hashum's family included Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.
Bani's family included Maadai, Amram, Uel,
as well as Benaiah, Bedeiah, Cheluhi,
Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib,
Mattaniah, Mattenai, Jaasu,
Bani, Binnui, Shimei,
Shelemiah, Nathan, Adaiah,
Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai,
Azarel, Shelemiah, Shemariah,
and Shallum, Amariah, and Joseph.
Nebo's family included Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Iddo, Joel, and Benaiah.
All these men had married foreign women. Some of the wives had borne children.
